Clinical Reference

Chronic Kidney Disease

On this page
Chronic kidney disease = abnormal kidney structure or function present for >3 months — an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or markers of damage (albuminuria ACR ≥30 mg/g, sediment, electrolyte or imaging abnormalities) — with implications for health. Staged by Cause · GFR (G1–G5) · Albuminuria (A1–A3).
CGA staging (KDIGO 2024) eGFR <60 or ACR ≥30 > 3 mo #1 killer is cardiovascular, not dialysis 4 pillars: RASi · SGLT2i · finerenone · GLP-1
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story of a failing filter

The kidney is 1–1.5 million nephrons, each a glomerular filter feeding a tubule. When nephrons are lost — to diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, cysts, or obstruction — the survivors are recruited to do the missing work. They hyperfilter: the afferent (upstream) arteriole dilates and the efferent (downstream) arteriole constricts under angiotensin II, raising pressure inside the glomerular tuft. This keeps total GFR up in the short term, but the high intraglomerular pressure batters the delicate filtration barrier. Podocytes detach, protein leaks into the urine (albuminuria), and the mesangium scars — glomerulosclerosis. Fewer functioning nephrons remain, the survivors hyperfilter harder, and the cycle accelerates. This is the final common pathway of virtually all progressive CKD, regardless of the initial insult.

A team where members keep quitting. The remaining workers cover the extra shifts (hyperfiltration) and burn out faster (glomerulosclerosis), so more quit — a vicious spiral. Every disease-modifying drug in CKD works by reducing the workload on the survivors so they last longer.
The final common pathway of CKD and where each drug class interrupts it. RASi and SGLT2i both lower intraglomerular pressure — from opposite ends of the capillary.
The nephron — glomerulus (filter) feeding the tubule. CKD is the progressive loss of these units and scarring of the survivors.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — KidneyStructures PioM.svg · Piotr Michał Jaworski; PioM EN DE PL · CC BY-SA 3.0
Glomerular scarring on histology — the structural endpoint of sustained hyperfiltration and injury.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Collapsing glomerulopathy - high mag.jpg · Nephron · CC BY-SA 3.0
The through-line of this whole guide: ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole → drop intraglomerular pressure from the downstream side. SGLT2 inhibitors restore tubuloglomerular feedback → constrict the afferent arteriole → drop pressure from the upstream side. Finerenone blocks mineralocorticoid-receptor–driven inflammation and fibrosis. GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce inflammation, weight and glycemia. Together they slow nephron loss — they don't regrow kidney.

🧪

The downstream consequences — why CKD patients get sick

As functioning renal mass falls, the kidney's non-filtration jobs fail one by one. Understanding each explains the drugs and the labs you'll trend.

System that failsMechanismClinical result
Salt & water balanceFewer nephrons excrete Na⁺/water; RAAS stays activatedVolume overload, hypertension, edema, heart failure
Potassium excretionDistal tubular K⁺ secretion falls; worsened by RASi, low aldosteroneHyperkalemia (life-threatening arrhythmia)
Acid excretionReduced ammoniagenesis and H⁺ excretionMetabolic acidosis (muscle wasting, bone loss, faster CKD progression)
Erythropoietin (EPO)Peritubular fibroblasts stop making EPO; iron sequestered by hepcidinNormocytic anemia → fatigue, LVH
Mineral & bone (CKD-MBD)↓Phosphate excretion → ↑FGF23 → ↓1,25-vitamin D → ↓Ca²⁺ → ↑PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)Renal osteodystrophy, vascular calcification, fractures
Uremic toxin clearanceRetention of urea and hundreds of middle moleculesUremia: nausea, pruritus, encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction
Diabetic kidney disease — the leading cause of CKD/ESKD. Chronic hyperglycemia drives hyperfiltration and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson).
Source: Wikimedia Commons — ACE inhibitors and Diabetic Nephropathy.png · Koshur1 · CC0
Urine dipstick — albuminuria is both an early marker of glomerular injury and an independent driver of progression and CV risk.

🗂️

Classification & staging — the KDIGO C-G-A system

KDIGO 2024 stages CKD by three axes: Cause, GFR category, and Albuminuria category. eGFR is estimated with the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation (race-free); cystatin C (eGFRcr-cys) is recommended to confirm when a precise value changes management.

GFR categoryeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)Term
G1≥90Normal or high (needs a damage marker to be CKD)
G260–89Mildly decreased (needs a damage marker to be CKD)
G3a45–59Mildly–moderately decreased
G3b30–44Moderately–severely decreased
G415–29Severely decreased
G5<15Kidney failure (add "D" if on dialysis)
Albuminuria categoryACR (mg/g)Term
A1<30Normal to mildly increased
A230–300Moderately increased (formerly "microalbuminuria")
A3>300Severely increased (formerly "macroalbuminuria")

The two axes combine into the KDIGO "heat map" risk grid below — the single most useful picture in nephrology. Risk of progression, ESKD, and death rises as you move down (falling GFR) and right (rising albuminuria). Note that albuminuria drives risk independently of GFR: a G1A3 patient (normal eGFR, heavy proteinuria) is higher-risk than a G3aA1 patient.

KDIGO heat map (schematic). Green = low risk; amber = moderate; red = high; deep red = very high. Both falling GFR and rising albuminuria push risk up — independently. Use the interactive staging calculator in the Clinic tab to place a patient.

Assess

Presentation & who to screen

🔍

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

CKD is usually silent until it is advanced — most patients are found on a routine metabolic panel or a screening urine ACR, not by symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they trace directly to the failing functions above. Frequencies below apply to symptomatic/advanced (G4–G5) disease.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Asymptomatic (found on labs)~80–90% earlyKidneys have enormous reserve; GFR falls well below 60 before symptoms emerge. This is why screening — not waiting for symptoms — finds CKD.
Fatigue / weakness~70–80% (advanced)Anemia (↓EPO) + uremic toxins + metabolic acidosis reduce oxygen delivery and muscle function.
Hypertension~75–90%Sodium/water retention + RAAS activation. Both a cause and a consequence of CKD — a bidirectional accelerator.
Edema / weight gain~40–60%Reduced Na⁺/water excretion → volume expansion; nephrotic-range proteinuria lowers oncotic pressure.
Nocturia~40–50%Loss of urinary concentrating ability → obligate solute diuresis at night.
Pruritus~20–40% (advanced)Uremic toxins, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and calcium-phosphate deposition irritate cutaneous nerves.
Nausea / anorexia / metallic taste~20–35% (advanced)Uremic gastrointestinal irritation; a classic sign that dialysis may be needed soon.
Restless legs / cramps~10–15%Uremic neuropathy, electrolyte shifts (Ca/Mg/PO₄), iron deficiency.
Uremic encephalopathy / pericarditis / bleeding<10% (G5)Severe toxin retention: asterixis/confusion, friction rub, platelet dysfunction. Each is a dialysis indication.
The most common "presentation" of CKD is an abnormal number on a lab you ordered for another reason. Two thresholds define it: eGFR <60 or ACR ≥30 — confirmed on a repeat ≥90 days apart to satisfy the ">3 months" chronicity criterion and separate CKD from AKI.

🎯

Who to screen — and with what

There is no universal population screening recommendation. The USPSTF (2012, reaffirmed as an "I" statement) found insufficient evidence to assess screening for CKD in asymptomatic adults. However, KDIGO 2024 and ADA 2024 recommend targeted annual screening of high-risk groups with both eGFR and urine ACR (a spot urine — first-morning is ideal):

  • Diabetes (type 2 at diagnosis, type 1 after 5 years) — annually (ADA 2024).
  • Hypertension — at diagnosis and periodically.
  • Cardiovascular disease, heart failure.
  • Family history of kidney failure, or hereditary kidney disease (e.g., ADPKD).
  • Age >60, obesity, recurrent AKI, nephrotoxic exposures (NSAIDs, PPIs long-term, lithium), high-risk ancestry, or APOL1 high-risk genotype.
Screen with both axes. eGFR alone misses the G1/G2 A3 patient (normal filtration, heavy proteinuria) who is at high risk. A urine ACR is far superior to a dipstick — it detects and quantifies moderately increased albuminuria the dipstick cannot see.

Treat

Chronic management — slow progression & cut CV risk

💊

The 4 pillars — first-line → escalation

Modern CKD care is built on foundational risk-factor control (BP, glycemia, lipids, lifestyle) plus four disease-modifying drug pillars layered on top, each proven to slow eGFR decline and reduce cardiorenal events. Layer them — they are additive and complementary.

The layered approach to albuminuric CKD (KDIGO 2024). Foundation first; then stack the pillars for which the patient qualifies.
1
Foundation — BP, glucose, lipids, lifestyle
Every CKD patient, from day one.
▾
Lowering systemic and intraglomerular pressure and correcting the metabolic drivers reduces the mechanical and inflammatory battering of the surviving nephrons.

  • Blood pressure: KDIGO 2021 target SBP <120 mmHg by standardized office measurement, if tolerated (2B, driven by SPRINT). This target only applies to properly measured BP — casual cuff readings should not be pushed to <120.
  • Glycemia (if diabetic): individualized HbA1c ~6.5–8.0% per KDIGO 2022 — lower for young/short-duration, higher (up to 8%) for advanced CKD/hypoglycemia risk. SGLT2i and metformin (if eGFR ≥30) are preferred agents.
  • Lipids (KDIGO 2013): statin (or statin/ezetimibe) for all CKD adults ≥50 yr with eGFR <60 not on dialysis; and ≥50 with eGFR ≥60; and 18–49 with a risk enhancer (CAD, DM, prior stroke, or 10-yr coronary risk >10%). Fire-and-forget — no LDL treat-to-target, no repeat titration. Do not initiate a statin de novo in a dialysis patient.
  • Lifestyle: sodium <2 g/day, protein ~0.8 g/kg/day (not lower — avoid malnutrition), smoking cessation, weight management, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, IV contrast when avoidable, aminoglycosides).
2
Pillar 1 — RAAS blockade (ACEi or ARB)
For albuminuria (A2/A3), especially with diabetes.
▾
ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, dropping intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria — the downstream valve on the glomerular capillary. This is why the expected small (<30%) creatinine bump is not harmful: it reflects the intended pressure drop, not injury.

DrugStartTitration → Target/MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant
Lisinopril (ACEi, default)10 mg dailyDouble q2–4 wk → max 40 mg/dayBlocks ANG II formation → efferent dilation → ↓glomerular pressure & albuminuriaCough → switch to an ARB
Ramipril (ACEi)2.5 mg daily→ 5 → 10 mg/daySame class; evidence base in HOPE/proteinuric CKDAngioedema → ARB (with caution) or non-RAAS
Losartan (ARB, default alt)50 mg daily→ 100 mg/dayBlocks AT₁ receptor — same hemodynamic effect, no bradykinin coughBilateral RAS, pregnancy, K⁺ >5.5 refractory → stop
Valsartan / Telmisartan (ARB)80 / 40 mg→ 320 / 80 mgRENAAL/IDNT proved renoprotection with ARBs in diabetic nephropathy—

Titrate to the highest tolerated approved dose — trial benefit came at max doses (KDIGO 2024, 1B). Check BMP (Cr, K⁺) 2–4 weeks after start/increase.

Handling the creatinine bump & K⁺A rise in creatinine ≤30% (eGFR fall ≤25%) is acceptable — continue and recheck. If Cr rises >30%: hunt for reversible causes (volume depletion, NSAIDs, other RAAS agents), then halve the dose and recheck in 1–2 weeks. For hyperkalemia (K⁺ 5.5–5.9): dietary K⁺ restriction, add/increase a loop or thiazide diuretic, correct acidosis, and add a K⁺ binder (patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to stay on the RASi rather than reflexively stopping it. Never combine ACEi + ARB (or + direct renin inhibitor) — more hyperkalemia/AKI, no benefit (ONTARGET).
3
Pillar 2 — SGLT2 inhibitor
For nearly all CKD with eGFR ≥20 + albuminuria — diabetic or not.
▾
By blocking proximal glucose/Na⁺ reabsorption, SGLT2i deliver more Na⁺ to the macula densa → restore tubuloglomerular feedback → constrict the afferent arteriole → drop intraglomerular pressure from the upstream side (complementary to RAAS). Plus natriuresis, weight/BP reduction, and less tubular oxygen demand.

DrugStartTargetWhy / thresholdsCautions
Dapagliflozin (default)10 mg daily10 mg daily (no titration)DAPA-CKD: HR 0.61 for kidney/CV composite. Initiate if eGFR ≥20; continue until dialysis/transplant even as eGFR falls.Hold during acute illness/surgery ("sick-day rule"); genital mycotic infection risk
Empagliflozin10 mg daily10 mg dailyEMPA-KIDNEY: HR 0.72; broadest eGFR range (20–45, or 45–90 with ACR ≥200); 54% non-diabeticAvoid in type 1 DM / high DKA risk; expect a reversible early eGFR dip — don't stop
The eGFR "dip" is expected and good. An acute 3–5 mL/min fall in the first weeks reflects the intended afferent constriction, mirrors the ACEi bump, and predicts long-term benefit. Do not discontinue for it.

4
Pillar 3 — Nonsteroidal MRA (finerenone)
T2DM + CKD with residual albuminuria despite max RASi + SGLT2i.
▾
Finerenone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor's inflammatory and pro-fibrotic signaling in the kidney and heart — a different lever than the hemodynamic pillars. Less hyperkalemia and no gynecomastia vs steroidal spironolactone.

DrugStart (by eGFR)Titration → TargetK⁺ gateEvidence
FinerenoneeGFR 25–<60 → 10 mg; eGFR ≥60 → 20 mg dailyRecheck K⁺ & eGFR at 4 wk; up-titrate 10→20 mg if K⁺ ≤4.8 & eGFR stable → target 20 mg/dayDo NOT start if K⁺ >5.0. Hold if K⁺ >5.5; restart 10 mg when K⁺ ≤5.0. Don't initiate if eGFR <25.FIDELIO-DKD & FIGARO-DKD: ↓kidney & CV events in diabetic CKD
5
Pillar 4 — GLP-1 receptor agonist
T2DM + CKD, especially with obesity or needing more glucose lowering.
▾
Beyond glucose and weight, GLP-1 RAs reduce renal and systemic inflammation and albuminuria. FLOW (2024) proved a hard renal/CV benefit in diabetic CKD.

DrugStartTitration → TargetWhy it worksCautions
Semaglutide (SC)0.25 mg weekly ×4 wk→ 0.5 → 1.0 mg weekly (FLOW maintenance)FLOW: HR 0.76 for major kidney/CV events (24% RRR); ↓albuminuria ~38%; ↓all-cause mortality 20%GI intolerance; avoid with personal/family MTC or MEN2; hold peri-operatively (gastroparesis/aspiration risk)
Order of assembly for diabetic albuminuric CKD: RASi (max tolerated) + SGLT2i as the base, then add finerenone for residual albuminuria with normal K⁺, and GLP-1 RA for additional glycemic/weight/CV benefit. Each pillar targets a distinct mechanism — they stack.

🩹

Treating the complications — anemia, CKD-MBD, acidosis

Anemia of CKD is normocytic, from ↓EPO and functional iron deficiency (hepcidin traps iron). Work up other causes first (B12/folate, blood loss).

  • Iron first (KDIGO 2012): for non-dialysis CKD with Hb below target, give a trial of iron if TSAT ≤30% and ferritin ≤500 ng/mL. Oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg or IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose, iron sucrose) if oral fails/not absorbed.
  • ESA (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin): start when Hb <10 g/dL (after replacing iron), and do not deliberately maintain Hb >11.5 g/dL — higher targets increased stroke/death (TREAT, CHOIR, Normal Hematocrit). Never target normal Hb.
  • HIF-PH inhibitors (daprodustat): oral alternative to ESAs (ASCEND trials) — raise endogenous EPO; option in selected patients.

CKD-MBD: as phosphate excretion falls, FGF23 and PTH rise and active vitamin D falls → secondary hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vascular calcification. Manage in this order:

  • Dietary phosphate restriction (limit processed foods/additives) first.
  • Phosphate binders with meals — non-calcium preferred to avoid calcium load/vascular calcification (KDIGO 2017): sevelamer carbonate 800–1600 mg PO TID; lanthanum carbonate 500–1000 mg TID; ferric citrate (also adds iron). Calcium acetate 667 mg (2 tabs TID) — restrict dose.
  • Active vitamin D / calcitriol 0.25 mcg daily (or paricalcitol) for rising PTH after controlling phosphate/replacing 25-OH D.
  • Calcimimetics (cinacalcet start 30 mg daily → up to 180 mg; or IV etelcalcetide) for secondary hyperparathyroidism on dialysis. Target dialysis PTH ~2–9× the upper limit of normal (KDIGO 2017).

Metabolic acidosis accelerates muscle wasting, bone loss, and CKD progression. Treat with oral sodium bicarbonate (e.g., 650 mg PO BID–TID, titrate) to keep serum bicarbonate ≥22 mmol/L (KDIGO — historically intervene <22; the 2024 update supports treating when HCO₃⁻ falls below the low-normal range). Watch for the sodium/volume load worsening hypertension. Veverimer (acid binder) is investigational.

Chronic hyperkalemia (limits life-saving RASi): low-K⁺ diet, loop/thiazide diuretic, correct acidosis, stop other K⁺-raising drugs (NSAIDs, trimethoprim, non-selective β-blockers). Potassium binders for persistent K⁺ >5.0–5.5 to preserve RASi: patiromer 8.4 g daily (titrate) or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g TID ×48h then 10 g daily. Older sodium polystyrene sulfonate is less favored (GI necrosis risk, slow onset).

Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

How often to check eGFR + ACR (by KDIGO risk)

KDIGO ties monitoring frequency to risk category — the number is the recommended times per year to check eGFR and ACR.

CategoryMonitoring frequency
G1–G2 A1 (low risk, only if CKD present)Once yearly (or per underlying condition)
G3a A1 / G1–2 A2 (moderate)~1×/year
G3b A1 / G3a A2 / G1–2 A3 (high)~2×/year
G4–G5, or any A3 with low GFR (very high)~3–4×/year (every 1–3 months)
  • After starting/titrating a RASi, SGLT2i, finerenone, or diuretic: BMP (Cr, K⁺) at 2–4 weeks.
  • Anemia: Hb every 3–6 months (G3), more often if on ESA. CKD-MBD labs: Ca/PO₄/PTH interval shortens by stage.
  • Vaccinate: influenza yearly, pneumococcal, hepatitis B (higher/repeat dosing; check titers — needed before dialysis), COVID-19, RSV per age.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change CKD — and its management

ComorbidityEffect on CKD courseEffect on management
Diabetes#1 cause of ESKD; hyperfiltration + nodular glomerulosclerosis accelerate lossPrioritize RASi + SGLT2i + finerenone/GLP-1; A1c ~7% individualized; metformin only if eGFR ≥30 (hold if ≥45→acute illness)
Hypertension2nd cause; nephrosclerosis; bidirectional acceleratorSBP <120 (standardized); RASi if albuminuric; loop diuretic once eGFR <30 (thiazides lose potency)
Heart failureCardiorenal syndrome; congestion ↓renal perfusionSGLT2i benefit both organs; careful diuresis; RASi/ARNI shared; watch K⁺ with MRA + RASi
CAD / prior MICKD is a CAD risk equivalent — CV death, not dialysis, is the usual endpointStatin regardless of LDL; caution with contrast (pre/post hydration); avoid nephrotoxins
GoutCommon; urate handling impairedAllopurinol dose-adjust & titrate to urate target; avoid NSAIDs for flares (colchicine dose-reduced, steroids)
ObesityDrives hyperfiltration, diabetes, HTNGLP-1 RA dual benefit; weight loss reduces albuminuria
Drugs to avoid or use with caution in CKD:
  • NSAIDs — afferent constriction → AKI-on-CKD, blunt RASi/diuretics, hyperkalemia. Avoid.
  • Iodinated & gadolinium contrast — contrast-associated AKI risk; gadolinium (esp. older linear agents) → nephrogenic systemic fibrosis at eGFR <30. Weigh necessity; hydrate.
  • Metformin — contraindicated if eGFR <30; lactic acidosis risk. Hold for acute illness/contrast.
  • Aminoglycosides, IV vancomycin (untrended), amphotericin, cisplatin, tenofovir (TDF), calcineurin inhibitors — nephrotoxic; dose-adjust and monitor.
  • Renally cleared drugs needing adjustment: gabapentin/pregabalin (sedation/myoclonus), many DOACs, LMWH (accumulates <30 → prefer UFH or anti-Xa dosing), digoxin, opioids (morphine/codeine metabolites accumulate — prefer other agents), certain antibiotics.
  • Bowel prep with sodium phosphate — acute phosphate nephropathy. Avoid.
Prevent

USPSTF & prevention

🛡️

Grade A/B services that protect these patients

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AScreen for and treat hypertensionAdults ≥18 — the 2nd leading cause of CKD
BScreen for type 2 diabetes / prediabetesAdults 35–70 with overweight/obesity — the #1 cause of CKD
BStatin for primary CV preventionAdults 40–75 with ≥1 CVD risk factor & 10-yr risk ≥7.5–10%
BTobacco cessation counseling + pharmacotherapyAll adults who smoke
IScreening for CKD in asymptomatic adults — insufficient evidence (not "against," just unproven at population level)General asymptomatic adults (USPSTF 2012)

The USPSTF does not endorse general CKD screening, but strongly supports screening/treating its two biggest drivers (diabetes, hypertension). KDIGO/ADA fill the gap with targeted ACR + eGFR screening of high-risk groups.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Nephrology referral & ED red flags

Refer to nephrology (KDIGO 2024) for any of:

  • eGFR <30 (G4–G5) — refer to plan for kidney replacement / conservative care ("at G4, the patient meets the nephrologist").
  • ACR ≥300 mg/g (A3) or albuminuria with hematuria.
  • Rapid progression — sustained eGFR decline >5 mL/min/year, or a drop across a GFR category with ≥25% loss from baseline.
  • CKD with refractory hypertension (≥4 agents), persistent K⁺ >5.5, or CKD-MBD abnormalities.
  • Suspected inherited or immunologic kidney disease; recurrent/extensive nephrolithiasis; AKI-on-CKD.
Send to ED / admit now: symptomatic hyperkalemia or K⁺ ≥6.5 (or ECG changes); pulmonary edema/refractory volume overload; severe metabolic acidosis; uremic symptoms (encephalopathy, pericarditis, intractable nausea); or a rapid unexplained rise in creatinine (AKI-on-CKD).
Vein preservation matters early. Once eGFR heads toward 20, protect the non-dominant arm — no BP cuffs, IVs, or PICCs — to preserve veins for a future AV fistula. "Fistula first."

🛏️ Wards — the decompensated CKD patient
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria — the complications, not the number

Patients are rarely admitted for a chronically low eGFR itself. Admit for the acute decompensations of CKD:

  • Severe hyperkalemia — K⁺ ≥6.0–6.5 or any ECG changes.
  • Volume overload / pulmonary edema not responsive to outpatient diuretics.
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ <15, pH <7.2) or mixed disorders.
  • Uremic symptoms — encephalopathy, pericarditis, intractable nausea/vomiting, bleeding.
  • AKI-on-CKD with a rapid creatinine rise, oliguria, or a new dialysis indication.
  • Symptomatic ESKD needing dialysis initiation / access failure (clotted fistula, catheter infection).
The first bedside question in a CKD admission: is this their chronic baseline, or AKI-on-CKD? Get the baseline creatinine, review the trajectory, assess volume, and screen for the reversible "AEIOU" dialysis indications immediately.

Treat

Acute management ladders

💊

The three inpatient emergencies of CKD

Sequence: protect the heart → shift K⁺ in → remove K⁺ from the body.

StepDrug / doseOnsetWhy it works
1. Stabilize membraneCalcium gluconate 1–2 g IV (or CaCl₂ via central line); repeat if ECG changes persist1–3 minRaises myocyte threshold potential — does NOT lower K⁺; buys time. Give for any ECG change or K⁺ ≥6.5.
2. Shift inRegular insulin 10 units IV + D50 (25 g); recheck glucose15–30 minDrives K⁺ into cells via Na-K-ATPase. Give dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia (the #1 complication).
2. Shift inAlbuterol 10–20 mg nebulized30 minβ₂ agonism shifts K⁺ intracellularly — additive to insulin.
3. RemoveFurosemide IV if making urine; K⁺ binder (SZC 10 g / patiromer); hemodialysis if refractory/oligoanurichrs / immediate (HD)Only these actually remove potassium. In ESKD/oligoanuria, dialysis is definitive.
BicarbonateIV bicarbonate is not a reliable acute K⁺-lowering agent unless the patient is significantly acidotic; don't rely on it as a primary shift.

Loop diuretics are first-line; CKD patients are loop-resistant and need higher doses to deliver enough drug to the tubule. Thiazides lose efficacy once eGFR <30 but add synergy for resistance.

DrugStart (in CKD)Titration → ceilingNotes
Furosemide (default)40–80 mg IVDouble per dose → up to 160–200 mg IV; convert to infusion if neededPO:IV ≈ 2:1 (oral bioavailability ~50%). Advanced CKD needs the higher ceilings.
Bumetanide1–2 mg IV→ up to ~10 mg/day1 mg bumetanide ≈ 40 mg furosemide; more reliable oral absorption.
Torsemide20 mg IV/PO→ up to ~200 mg/day~2:1 vs furosemide; best, most consistent oral bioavailability (~80%).
Metolazone (add-on)2.5–5 mg PO→ 10 mgGive 30 min before the loop for sequential nephron blockade in resistance. Watch for profound K⁺/Na⁺ loss.
If a patient is oligoanuric or has refractory overload despite max IV loops + metolazone, diuretics have failed — the answer is ultrafiltration / dialysis, not more furosemide.

For symptomatic or severe metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ <15–18): IV sodium bicarbonate — e.g., an isotonic bicarbonate infusion (150 mEq in D5W) titrated to raise HCO₃⁻ toward ≥22, watching Na⁺/volume. Chronic outpatient management uses oral bicarbonate. Refractory acidosis with volume intolerance is a dialysis indication.

Monitor

What to trend daily

📈

The daily CKD checklist

  • K⁺ and HCO₃⁻ — the two that kill; recheck after each intervention.
  • Creatinine trajectory vs baseline — improving (AKI resolving) or worsening (approaching dialysis)?
  • Volume: daily weight, strict I/O, exam (JVP, crackles, edema), O₂ requirement.
  • Urine output — oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) predicts need for renal replacement.
  • Uremic signs — mental status, asterixis, pericardial rub, appetite, nausea.
  • Med list — re-check renal dosing daily as eGFR changes; restart held cardio-renal drugs when stable.
Escalate

When to call ICU / dialysis

⬆️

Urgent dialysis & ICU triggers — "AEIOU"

LetterIndication for urgent dialysisConcrete trigger
AAcidosisSevere metabolic acidosis refractory to medical therapy (e.g., pH <7.1)
EElectrolytesHyperkalemia refractory to medical management or with ECG changes (K⁺ ≥6.5)
IIntoxicationsDialyzable toxins — methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, lithium ("I STUMBLED")
OOverloadVolume overload / pulmonary edema refractory to diuretics
UUremiaUremic pericarditis, encephalopathy/asterixis, uremic bleeding, or intractable symptoms
Escalate to ICU for: hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors, refractory pulmonary edema needing BiPAP/intubation, life-threatening hyperkalemia with arrhythmia, or the need for CRRT in a patient too unstable for intermittent hemodialysis.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: K⁺ <5.5 and stable off acute therapy; euvolemic on a stable oral diuretic regimen; acidosis corrected/stable; creatinine at or trending to baseline; uremic symptoms resolved; a clear outpatient nephrology follow-up and (if new ESKD) a dialysis plan and access. Reconcile renally dosed meds and confirm which cardio-renal drugs to resume.

Home

Back to baseline, independent, reliable follow-up; established or scheduled outpatient dialysis if ESKD.

Home health

Needs nursing for new meds, weights, wound/access care, or IV iron infusions at home.

SNF

Deconditioned, needs 24h skilled nursing (e.g., new dialysis + rehab, complex med management), <3h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Functional decline but can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., dialysis + vent weaning, non-healing access infection) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Conservative (non-dialytic) management chosen, or frailty/limited prognosis; symptom-focused. A valid pathway — median survival on conservative care can approach that of dialysis in the very elderly/frail.
🫀 ICU — renal replacement & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers & severe presentations

🚨

When CKD belongs in the unit

Severe presentationWhat it is / ICU action
Life-threatening hyperkalemiaK⁺ ≥6.5 with wide QRS/arrhythmia — continuous ECG, IV calcium, shift therapy, urgent HD/CRRT; central access.
Refractory pulmonary edemaFlash edema in oligoanuric ESKD — NIV/intubation + urgent ultrafiltration/HD; diuretics futile if anuric.
Severe uremiaUremic pericarditis (tamponade risk), encephalopathy, or bleeding — urgent dialysis; give DDAVP for uremic bleeding.
Hemodynamic instability + AKI/ESKDShock precluding intermittent HD → CRRT; treat underlying cause (sepsis, cardiogenic).
Dialyzable intoxicationToxic alcohols, severe salicylate, lithium, metformin-associated lactic acidosis — emergent HD.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Vascular access for RRT: non-tunneled temporary HD catheter (internal jugular preferred) for urgent/short-term; tunneled catheter for weeks; plan an AV fistula (or graft) for durable access — "fistula first." Protect an existing fistula arm — no BP cuffs, sticks, or lines in it.
  • Trend: K⁺ and pH/HCO₃⁻ frequently around RRT; ionized calcium (esp. with citrate anticoagulation on CRRT); phosphate (can fall on continuous therapy); fluid balance hourly.
  • Anticoagulation for CRRT: regional citrate (preferred; monitor ionized Ca and for citrate accumulation in liver failure) or systemic heparin.
A central venous dialysis catheter provides immediate access for urgent RRT, but carries infection and central-vein stenosis risk — a bridge to a fistula, not a destination.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Demerskatheter in der Computertomographie 79M - CT axial - 001.jpg · Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 4.0
A surgically created arteriovenous fistula — the preferred durable hemodialysis access ("fistula first"); needs weeks to months to mature.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Schema fistule arterio-veineuse - AV fistula.jpg · Pravdaz · CC BY-SA 3.0
Support

Hemodynamic support

💉

Pressors in the CKD/RRT patient

CKD patients arrive in the ICU in shock like anyone else (often sepsis or cardiogenic). Pressor choice follows standard critical-care principles; the CKD twist is intradialytic hypotension and the need to maintain a mean arterial pressure that preserves residual renal function and RRT tolerance.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line for septic/distributive shock; maintain MAP ≥65
VasopressinV1 receptor0.03 units/min (fixed)↑SVR (catecholamine-sparing)Add-on to norepinephrine; useful in acidemia where catecholamines lose potency
Epinephrineβ1/β2 + α10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR, ↑HRRefractory shock; anaphylaxis
Dobutamineβ1 > β22.5–10 mcg/kg/min↑contractility, ↑COCardiorenal / cardiogenic shock with low output
In severe acidemia (common in uremic/RRT patients), catecholamine receptors are less responsive — correcting pH (via dialysis/bicarbonate) and adding vasopressin can restore pressor effect. Avoid over-aggressive fluids in oligoanuric ESKD — you cannot "pee off" the excess; it goes to the lungs.

Support

RRT modality — IHD vs CRRT vs SLED

🌊

Choosing the dialysis modality

Modality is chosen by hemodynamics and goals, not by "which clears more."

IHD
Intermittent HD
3–4 h sessions; fast clearance. For hemodynamically stable patients; urgent hyperkalemia/toxin removal.
CRRT
Continuous (CVVH/CVVHDF)
24 h/day, slow fluid/solute removal. For shock/pressor-dependent, cerebral edema, severe fluid overload needing gentle UF.
SLED
Prolonged intermittent (6–12 h)
Hybrid — hemodynamic tolerance of CRRT with lower cost/anticoagulation burden.
PD
Peritoneal
Continuous, no anticoagulation/vascular access; slower — used in selected/chronic and resource-limited settings.
Timing of initiation (STARRT-AKI, 2020)In critically ill AKI without an emergent indication, an accelerated RRT start showed no mortality benefit and more dialysis dependence vs a standard/watchful strategy. Translation: don't rush to dialyze for the number alone — treat the AEIOU emergencies, otherwise you can safely wait and watch.
A hemodialysis machine — blood is pumped across a semipermeable membrane against dialysate to remove solutes and fluid. In the ICU, the same principle runs continuously (CRRT) for unstable patients.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Dialog-dialysis-machine-b-braun.jpg · Jonas@sodratornet.se · CC BY-SA 4.0
Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum as the membrane — no vascular access or systemic anticoagulation, a home-based option for durable therapy.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — 202406 Peritoneal Dialysis APD Child.svg · DataBase Center for Life Science (DBCLS) · CC BY 4.0
Rescue

Advanced / definitive options

⚙️

Kidney replacement therapy pathways & complications

  • Chronic modality choice: in-center HD, home HD, or peritoneal dialysis — shared decision by lifestyle, cardiac stability, and support.
  • Kidney transplant — the best survival and quality-of-life option. Refer for evaluation and waitlist when eGFR ≤20 (can list pre-dialysis; pre-emptive transplant gives the best outcomes).
  • Conservative (non-dialytic) management — a legitimate, proactive choice for frail/elderly patients where dialysis may not extend meaningful life; focus on symptoms and quality of life with palliative support.
  • Complications to anticipate: dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (cerebral edema from too-rapid urea clearance in a first, aggressive session — go slow initially), intradialytic hypotension, catheter-related bloodstream infection, access thrombosis/stenosis, and air embolism.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade to the floor when: off vasopressors and hemodynamically stable; transitioned from CRRT to a tolerated intermittent HD schedule (or no longer needs RRT); K⁺ <5.5 and acid-base stable; respiratory status stable off NIV; and a durable access plan is in motion.
Not yet if…still pressor-dependent, requiring CRRT for hemodynamic intolerance of IHD, has an uncontrolled dialysis-access infection with bacteremia, or has labile potassium requiring continuous monitoring.

ICU disposition: most stabilize to the floor and then home or SNF with an outpatient dialysis chair. Those with prolonged ventilator/dialysis dependence may need LTAC; revisit goals of care in patients where dialysis is not improving quality or length of life.

Evidence

Landmark trials

📚

The trials that built modern CKD care

Trial (year)ResultWhy it matters
RENAAL (2001)Losartan ↓ doubling of Cr/ESKD by 16% in T2DM nephropathyEstablished ARBs as renoprotective — beyond BP lowering
IDNT (2001)Irbesartan slowed progression vs amlodipine/placeboCemented RAAS blockade as the foundation of diabetic CKD
SPRINT (2015)Intensive SBP <120 ↓ CV events & mortality (incl. CKD subgroup)Basis for KDIGO 2021 SBP <120 target (standardized)
CREDENCE (2019)Canagliflozin ↓ kidney failure/CV death by 30% in diabetic CKDFirst dedicated SGLT2i renal-outcome trial; opened the pillar
DAPA-CKD (2020)Dapagliflozin: composite HR 0.61; benefit regardless of diabetesExtended SGLT2i to non-diabetic CKD; NNT ≈19
EMPA-KIDNEY (2023)Empagliflozin: composite HR 0.72; broadest eGFR range; 54% non-DMWidened who qualifies (eGFR down to 20; ACR ≥200)
FIDELIO-DKD (2020)Finerenone ↓ kidney & CV events in diabetic CKDLaunched the nonsteroidal MRA pillar
FIGARO-DKD (2021)Finerenone ↓ CV events in earlier diabetic CKDExtended finerenone benefit across the CKD spectrum
FLOW (2024)Semaglutide: major kidney/CV events HR 0.76 (24% RRR)Established GLP-1 RA as a renal-protective pillar in diabetic CKD
TREAT / CHOIR (2006–09)Targeting higher Hb with ESAs ↑ stroke/CV harmWhy the ESA Hb ceiling is ~11.5, not "normal"
STARRT-AKI (2020)Accelerated RRT start: no mortality benefit, more dialysis dependenceDon't dialyze for the number alone — treat the AEIOU emergencies
Twelve pearls to carry: (1) CKD = eGFR<60 or ACR≥30 for >3 months. (2) Stage by C-G-A; albuminuria drives risk independent of GFR. (3) The #1 cause of death in CKD is cardiovascular, not dialysis. (4) The ACEi/ARB creatinine bump ≤30% is expected — keep going. (5) The SGLT2i eGFR "dip" is expected and predicts benefit. (6) SGLT2i now help non-diabetic CKD too. (7) Add a K⁺ binder to stay on RASi rather than stopping it. (8) Never combine ACEi + ARB. (9) Statins are fire-and-forget — no LDL target; don't start de novo on dialysis. (10) Loop diuretics need higher ceilings in CKD; thiazides fail below eGFR 30. (11) "Fistula first" — protect the veins early. (12) Refer at eGFR <30 or ACR ≥300; list for transplant at eGFR ≤20.
